An ibex is a type of wild goat that lives in rugged, steep, rocky mountain regions. It is not a farm goat or a domesticated animal — it is fully wild, built by nature to survive in some of the harshest and most dangerous landscapes on Earth.
What Does an Ibex Look Like?

The most striking feature of an ibex is its horns — large, curved, and ridged like a series of bumps or rings running along their length. These horns sweep dramatically backward over the animal's body and can grow remarkably long, sometimes exceeding a meter in the males. The ridges on the horns are not decorative; they mark the animal's age, somewhat like tree rings — one ridge typically forms each year of the ibex's life.

Male ibexes (called bucks) have much larger and more impressive horns than females (called does or nannies). The females have shorter, more slender horns. The body of an ibex is stocky and muscular, built for strength rather than speed. Their hooves are specially adapted — they have hard outer edges for gripping rock and soft, rubbery inner pads that act like natural suction cups on steep surfaces. This is what makes them extraordinary climbers.

An adult ibex typically stands about 65–100 cm at the shoulder (roughly the height of a large dog) and can weigh anywhere from 30 to 120 kg, depending on the species and sex.

Ibexes are found in mountains across Europe, Asia, and Africa. The exact location depends on the species:

  • Alpine ibex live in the Alps of Europe (Switzerland, France, Italy, Austria).
  • Nubian ibex live in the rocky deserts and mountains of northeastern Africa and the Middle East (like Egypt, Sudan, Israel, and Jordan).
  • Siberian ibex live across the mountains of Central Asia (from Russia through Mongolia and down to the Himalayas).
  • Spanish ibex (Iberian ibex) live in the Pyrenees and other mountain ranges of the Iberian Peninsula.
  • Walia ibex live in the Simien Mountains of Ethiopia, and are one of the rarest.

Regardless of the species, all ibexes share one thing in common: they prefer very high altitudes, often living at elevations above 3,000 metres. During summer, they climb even higher. In winter, they descend slightly to avoid the worst conditions, but they still stay in rocky, elevated terrain that most animals (and humans) cannot easily access.

Ibexes are among the most remarkable climbers in the animal kingdom. They can scale nearly vertical cliff faces with ease and confidence that seems almost impossible for an animal of their size. Their hooves do most of the work — the two "toes" of each hoof can spread apart to grip the rock, and the texture of the hoof sole provides friction. An ibex can stand on a ledge just a few centimetres wide without slipping.

This ability to climb vertical terrain is also their primary defence mechanism. When threatened by predators — wolves, snow leopards, eagles (which target young ibexes), or bears — they simply flee upward into terrain their predators cannot follow.

Ibexes are herbivores, meaning they eat only plant matter. Their diet includes grass, moss, herbs, flowers, shrubs, and leaves — whatever grows in their mountain environment. During the warmer months when food is plentiful, they eat abundantly and build up fat reserves. During harsh winters, when snow covers most of the vegetation, food becomes scarce and survival becomes the priority.

Ibexes have a multi-chambered stomach (like cows and goats) that allows them to digest tough, fibrous plant material efficiently. They often chew their cud — meaning they regurgitate partially digested food and chew it again to extract maximum nutrition.

Ibexes are social animals, but males and females largely live apart from each other for most of the year. Females and their young typically form their own herds. Males form separate bachelor herds. They only come together during the mating season (called the rut), which typically occurs in winter.

During the rut, males compete fiercely for the right to mate with females. They rear up on their hind legs and clash their massive horns together with tremendous force. These battles can be dramatic and loud, but are rarely fatal — the horns and thick skull of the ibex absorb much of the impact.

After mating, females carry their young for about 5–6 months and typically give birth to one or two kids in spring or early summer. The young ibexes are astonishingly capable from the very start — within hours of birth, a kid can already walk and even follow its mother across rocky terrain.

Ibexes have had a complicated history with humans. For centuries, they were heavily hunted — not just for their meat and hide, but because various parts of their body (horns, blood, stomach stones) were falsely believed to have medicinal powers in European folk medicine. This led to the Alpine ibex coming dangerously close to extinction by the early 19th century, with only a tiny population surviving in the Gran Paradiso region of what is now Italy, protected by the royal house of Savoy.

Thanks to conservation efforts, the Alpine ibex has since been successfully reintroduced across the Alps, and their numbers have recovered to tens of thousands. However, other species — particularly the Walia ibex — remain critically endangered today, with only a few hundred individuals left in the wild, threatened by habitat loss, illegal hunting, and human encroachment into their range.
The word ibex has three accepted plural forms: ibex (same as singular), ibexes, or the Latinised ibices. In everyday usage, "ibexes" is the most commonly used and easily understood plural.

An ibex is a wild, mountain-dwelling goat known for its spectacular curved ridged horns, extraordinary climbing ability, and hardy survival in some of Earth's most inhospitable mountain terrain. It is herbivorous, social in a sex-segregated way, and has several distinct species spread across Europe, Asia, and Africa. Its defining image — a sure-footed animal with great curving horns, standing calmly on a near-vertical cliff face thousands of metres above sea level — is one of the most iconic in the natural world.
